questions.question:
Choose the one word substitute for the below sentence.

Emily asked her friend, a person who has never been married called?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '4' i.e. Bachelor .

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The word **"Bachelor"** refers to a man who has never been married.
 
• **"Single"** refers to someone who is not in a relationship, but it does not necessarily indicate whether they have been married before.
 
• **"Celibate"** refers to someone who abstains from marriage or sexual activity for religious or personal reasons; it does not specifically mean they have never been married.
 
• **"Widower"** refers to a man whose spouse has died, indicating that he was previously married.

Correct sentence: *Emily asked her friend, a person who has never been married is called a **Bachelor**.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Usage in context:** The term "Bachelor" is often used to describe the marital status of a man who has never been married.
 
• **Distinction:** It is specific to men, while the equivalent term for women is "Spinster," though the latter is considered outdated and less commonly used.
</ul

• The phrase **"on the time"** is incorrect because it does not align with standard English usage.
 
• The correct phrase should be **"at the time"**, which is used to refer to a specific moment or point in time.

• **"On":** Used for days and dates. Example: "I have a meeting on Monday."
 
• **"In":** Used for longer periods like months, years, or centuries. Example: "She was born in July."
 
• **"At":** Used for specific points in time or specific places. Example: "The train arrives at 7 PM."
 
 
 
• **Contextual Correction:** Always match the preposition to the intended meaning in the sentence.

questions.question:
Choose the option that is the most appropriate conversion of the following sentence into Active Voice.

The students were made to rewrite the entire assignment.

options.text: The The teacher made the students rewrite the entire assignment.
The teacher makes the students rewrite the entire assignment.
The teacher is making the students rewrite the entire assignment.
The teacher has made the students rewrite the entire assignment.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is '1' i.e. The teacher made the students rewrite the entire assignment .

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The given sentence is in the **passive voice**, where the action is being done to the students.
 
• To convert the sentence into the **active voice**, the subject performing the action (the teacher) must be mentioned first.
 
• The **verb tense** must remain consistent when converting from passive to active voice. Here, "were made" (past tense passive) is converted to "made" (past tense active).

Correct sentence: *The teacher made the students rewrite the entire assignment*.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Active Voice:**

 
 
• **Definition:** The subject performs the action mentioned by the verb.
 
• **Example:** The teacher made the students rewrite the assignment.
 
• **Usage:** Active voice sentences are direct and concise.
 
 
 
• **Passive Voice:**
 
 
• **Definition:** The subject receives the action performed by the verb.
 
• **Example:** The students were made to rewrite the assignment.
 
• **Usage:** Passive voice is used when the focus is on the action rather than the subject.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The question requires converting a direct speech into **indirect narration**.
 
• To do this, certain grammatical changes are necessary:
 
 
• The **pronouns** are adjusted to match the subject of the speaker.
 
• The **tense** of the verbs is backshifted (e.g., "will" becomes "would," "must" becomes "had to").
 
• Time expressions are changed accordingly (e.g., "tomorrow" becomes "the day after").
 
 
 
• Thus, the phrase "You will get up early tomorrow..." in direct speech is converted to "He would get up early the day after..." in indirect speech.

Correct sentence: *Sohan said that he would get up early the day after to go for a morning walk as he had to qualify in the physical test.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Indirect Narration Rules:**
 
 
• **Pronoun Changes:** Pronouns in direct speech are adjusted to match the subject and object in the indirect sentence.
 
• **Tense Changes:** Verbs in direct speech are backshifted in indirect speech:
 
 
• "will" → "would"
 
• "must" → "had to"
 
 
 
• **Time and Place Changes:** Time expressions are modified for indirect narration:
 
 
• "tomorrow" → "the day after"

The student inquired what the deadline for the submission was.

options.text: The student said, "When is the deadline for submission?"

The students inquired, "What was the deadline for the submission?"
The student inquired, "What is the deadline for the submission?"

__
 
• Direct speech conveys the exact words spoken by the speaker, often enclosed in quotation marks.
 
• In this case, the student is directly asking about the deadline for submission, so the sentence in direct speech must retain the original tense and structure.
 
• The correct form is: "What is the deadline for the submission?" because it reflects the student's inquiry accurately.
 
• Option 4 matches the correct direct speech format and maintains the original question's tense (present simple).

• **Direct Speech:** Direct speech quotes the speaker's words exactly as they were spoken, often using quotation marks. Example: The student asked, "What is the deadline for the submission?"
 
• **Key Difference:** Tense changes often occur in indirect speech, while direct speech retains the original tense.

• Therefore, the correct prepositions to fill in the blanks are **on** for the first blank and **to** for the second blank.

Correct sentence: *The firm prides itself **on** quality service and adheres strictly **to** international standards.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

questions.question:

__
 
• The given sentence is written in the **passive voice**. To convert it into the **active voice**, the subject (the agent performing the action) must become explicit.
 
• In the passive sentence, the action is described as being performed, but the doer of the action is implied. The active voice specifies the doer directly.

• **Active Voice:**
 
 
• **Structure:** Subject + verb + object.
 
• **Example:** She read the book.

</ul

questions.question:

why is the verb "have" used instead of "has"?

__
 
• This question tests the rule of **Subject-Verb Agreement**.
 
• In the sentence: *"Silver **ornaments have** been a part..."* the noun **"ornaments"** is the head of the subject phrase.
 
• Since **"ornaments"** is a **plural countable noun**, it requires a plural verb (**have**).
 
• If the subject were simply "Silver" (uncountable), we would use "has," but here "Silver" acts as an adjective modifying the plural noun "ornaments."
 
• Why other options are incorrect: 
 
 
• **Option 2:** While "silver" is uncountable, it is not the functional subject here; "ornaments" is. If "silver" were the subject, the verb would be the singular "has."
 
• **Option 3:** "Collections" is part of the **object/complement** phrase ("part of... collections"), not the subject. The verb must agree with the subject that comes before it.
 
• **Option 4:** The sentence is in the **Present Perfect Tense** (active voice), not passive voice. "Have been" here indicates a state that started in the past and continues to the present.
 
 

Therefore, the correct answer is **1**.

 

**Analytical Insight:** *In competitive exams, examiners often place a singular noun (like "Silver") right before a plural subject (like "ornaments") to trick you. Always identify the **main noun** that the verb is actually describing.*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Subject-Verb Agreement:** The grammatical rule that the verb or verbs in a sentence must match the number, person, and gender of the subject.
 
• **Uncountable Nouns:** Nouns like *water, silver, advice* that cannot be counted and usually take a singular verb.
 
• **Countable Nouns:** Nouns like *ornament, book, chair* that can be pluralized and take plural verbs.

questions.question: In a row of boys, Deepak is 9th from the left and Kavya is 12th from the right. If they exchange their positions, Deepak becomes 18th from the left. What will be the position of Kavya from the right?

Kavya takes Deepak’s original position (9th from the left).

Position of Kavya from the right = 29 - 9 + 1 = 21.

So, Kavya is 21st from the right.

Hence, the correct answer is **"Option 2".**

questions.question: Who among the following is a Jnanpith Award-winning woman writer?
questions.solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Mahadevi Verma** was one of the most eminent writers of Hindi literature and a recipient of the prestigious **Jnanpith Award** in **1982**.
 
• She is widely regarded as a pioneer in modern Hindi literature and is considered one of the four pillars of Chhayavad poetry, alongside **Suryakant Tripathi 'Nirala,' Jai Shankar Prasad, and Sumitranandan Pant**.
 
• Her works often reflect themes of **feminism, individualism, and the human struggle**. She was known for her contributions to both poetry and prose.
 
• Mahadevi Verma's most famous works include **"Yama" (a poetry collection that won the Jnanpith Award)** and prose writings such as **"Aatmika" and "Smriti Ki Rekhayen."**
 
• She also earned the title of **"Modern Meera"** due to her spiritual and deeply emotional style of writing, which resonated with readers across generations.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Jnanpith Award:**

 
 
• The **Jnanpith Award** is one of India's highest literary honors, established in **1961** by the Bharatiya Jnanpith organization.
 
• It is awarded annually to an author for their outstanding contribution to literature in any of the **22 official languages** of India as per the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution.
 
• Recipients of the award are presented with a **citation, a shawl, and a cash prize**.
 
• The first recipient of the Jnanpith Award was **G. Sankara Kurup** in **Malayalam**. Mahadevi Verma became the first woman recipient of this award for her contributions in **Hindi literature**.
 
 
 
• **Other Options:**
 
 
• **Sarojini Naidu:** Known as the **"Nightingale of India"**, Sarojini Naidu was a poet and freedom fighter. Although she made significant contributions to Indian literature, she did not receive the Jnanpith Award.
 
• **Kamala Surayya:** Also known as **Kamala Das**, she was a renowned poet and writer who contributed to Malayalam and English literature. She received several awards but did not win the Jnanpith Award.
 
• **Subhadra Kumari Chauhan:** A famous Hindi poet known for her patriotic works such as **"Jhansi Ki Rani"**, Subhadra Kumari Chauhan did not receive the Jnanpith Award.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Mahadevi Verma's Work:**
 
 
• Her work is celebrated for its **lyrical beauty and depth**, often exploring themes of social reform, human emotions, and spirituality.
 
• She was also a strong advocate for **women’s rights** and often addressed issues of gender inequality in her writings.
 
• Mahadevi Verma's influence on Hindi literature and the Chhayavad movement has been profound and enduring.

• **Chhayavad Movement:**

 
 
• Chhayavad refers to the romanticism movement in Hindi literature, which emerged in the early 20th century.
 
• It is characterized by a focus on **nature, beauty, personal emotions, and spirituality**.
 
• Mahadevi Verma was one of the key figures in this movement, alongside Sumitranandan Pant, Jai Shankar Prasad, and Suryakant Tripathi 'Nirala'.
 
 
 
• **Legacy of Mahadevi Verma:**
 
 
• She was awarded numerous accolades, including the **Padma Bhushan** and the **Sahitya Akademi Fellowship**.
 
• She served as the editor of **"Chand" magazine**, contributing significantly to Hindi journalism and literature.
 
• In recognition of her contributions, institutions and awards have been established in her name to promote Hindi literature.

questions.question: The "Aatmanirbharta in Pulses" campaign, launched in Union Budget 2025, is a government mission spanning.___________years to achieve self-sufficiency in pulse production.

• The "**Aatmanirbharta in Pulses**" campaign was announced in the **Union Budget 2025** as a mission to achieve **self-sufficiency in pulse production**.
 
• The campaign spans a period of **6 years**, aiming to reduce India's dependence on pulse imports.
 
• India is one of the largest consumers and producers of pulses globally, but the domestic production often falls short of demand, necessitating imports.
 
• The campaign aligns with the broader vision of **Aatmanirbhar Bharat** (Self-Reliant India) promoted by the Indian government to strengthen domestic agriculture and food security.
 
• The program focuses on encouraging **pulse cultivation** through incentives such as **minimum support prices (MSP)**, subsidies on seeds and fertilizers, and advanced farming techniques.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Importance of Pulses in India:**

 
 
• Pulses are a crucial source of **protein** for a largely vegetarian population in India.
 
• They contribute significantly to **nutritional security** and are an essential component of Indian diets.
 
• Key pulses grown in India include **chickpeas**, **pigeon peas**, **mung beans**, and **lentils**.
 
 
 
• **Challenges in Pulse Production:**
 
 
• Fluctuating rainfall patterns due to **climate change** impact yields.
 
• High cost of inputs like **seeds, fertilizers, and irrigation**.
 
• Low adoption of modern farming techniques and inadequate access to **credit**.
 
 
 
• **Government Initiatives for Pulses:**
 
 
• The **National Food Security Mission (NFSM)** promotes pulse production through area expansion and productivity improvement.
 
• The government imports pulses and maintains a **buffer stock** to stabilize prices and ensure availability.
 
• Subsidies are provided on **high-yielding seeds** and **micro-irrigation systems**.
 
 
 
• **Global Context:**
 
 
• India is the **largest consumer** and one of the biggest producers of pulses but also relies on imports from countries like **Canada, Myanmar, and Australia**.
 
• The **Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO)** has recognized pulses as a critical crop for global food security.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Pulse Consumption in India:**

 
 
• The average per capita pulse consumption in India is around **22-24 kilograms per year**, contributing significantly to daily protein intake.
 
• Despite being a major producer, India imports **2-3 million tonnes** of pulses annually to meet domestic demand.
 
 
 
• **Economic Implications:**
 
 
• Pulses are a key component of the Indian agricultural economy, contributing to farmers' incomes and rural development.
 
• The government has implemented measures like **Price Stabilization Fund** to ensure remunerative prices for farmers and affordable rates for consumers.
 
 
 
• **Sustainability Aspect:**
 
 
• Pulses are **nitrogen-fixing crops** that enhance soil fertility, reducing the need for chemical fertilizers.
 
• Promoting pulse cultivation aligns with sustainable agricultural practices and environmental conservation.

• **Keibul Lamjao National Park** is located in the state of **Manipur**, India. It is renowned as the **only floating national park in the world**.
 
• This unique park is situated on the **Loktak Lake**, which is the largest freshwater lake in northeastern India, known for its distinctive floating islands called **phumdis**.
 
• The park is home to the **Sangai deer**, also known as the **Brow-antlered deer**, which is the state animal of Manipur and is classified as **Endangered** by the IUCN.

• **Phumdis** are floating biomass consisting of a heterogeneous mass of vegetation, soil, and organic matter in various stages of decomposition.
 
• These floating islands are found only in Loktak Lake and provide a unique ecosystem for flora and fauna.
 
• The phumdis support the livelihood of locals who use them for fishing and other activities.
 
 
 
• **Loktak Lake:**
 
 
• **Loktak Lake** is the largest freshwater lake in northeastern India and is often referred to as the **"Lifeline of Manipur"**.
 
• The lake plays a vital role in the socio-economic and ecological balance of the region, supporting agriculture, fishing, and hydropower generation.
 
• In 1990, Loktak Lake was designated as a **Ramsar site**, recognizing its international importance as a wetland.
 
 
 
• **Sangai Deer:**
 
 
• The **Sangai deer** is an endemic species found only in Manipur, primarily in Keibul Lamjao National Park.
 
• Known for its graceful movement, the deer is also called the **"Dancing Deer of Manipur"**.
 
• Conservation efforts are ongoing to protect this endangered species, which faces threats from habitat loss and poaching.
 
 
 
• **Biodiversity of Keibul Lamjao National Park:**
 
 
• The park is home to diverse fauna, including species like **hog deer**, **otters**, **waterfowl**, and many migratory birds.
 
• It also harbors several rare aquatic plants and serves as a critical habitat for fish and other aquatic organisms.
 
• The park's unique ecosystem makes it an important area for ecological research and conservation.

• **Geographical Significance:**

 
 
• Keibul Lamjao National Park is located on the southern shore of Loktak Lake, at an altitude of **768 meters above sea level**.
 
• Its unique floating habitat is critical for the survival of the Sangai deer and other endemic species.
 
 
 
• **Ecotourism Potential:**

• **‘Gurjari’ raga** is a classical raga in Indian music and is traditionally associated with the state of **Gujarat**.
 
• The name "Gurjari" is derived from "Gurjar," which historically refers to the region and people of Gujarat.
 
• This raga is known for its **melodic structure**, evoking emotions of devotion and peace, which aligns with the cultural essence of Gujarat.

• **Indian Classical Music:**

 
 
• Indian classical music has two major traditions: **Hindustani** (North Indian) and **Carnatic** (South Indian) music.
 
• Ragas are **melodic frameworks** used in both traditions to compose music, each raga having unique characteristics and emotional expressions.
 
• Ragas are often associated with specific **times of the day** or seasons, as well as particular moods.
 
• Gurjari raga belongs to the Hindustani tradition and is performed in devotional and folk music settings.
 
 
 
• **Music in Gujarat:**
 
 
• Gujarat has a rich musical heritage, blending **folk and classical traditions**.
 
• Folk music like Garba and Dandiya Raas, along with classical ragas like Gurjari, form the state's cultural identity.

• **Important Characteristics of Ragas:**
 
 
• A raga consists of a specific set of notes arranged in a **scale** that defines its melodic structure.
 
• Each raga has specific rules for ascending (Aaroh) and descending (Avroh) patterns.
 
• The emotional essence or "rasa" of a raga can evoke a wide range of feelings, such as devotion, joy, or melancholy.

questions.question: Who constructed the city of Tughlaqabad?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq**, the founder of the Tughlaq dynasty, is credited with constructing the city of **Tughlaqabad** in the early 14th century.
 
• The city was built in **1321** as a fortified settlement near Delhi and served as a defense against Mongol invasions, showcasing a strong military architectural style.
 
• Tughlaqabad is known for its **imposing stone walls**, massive fortifications, and strategic location overlooking the plains of Delhi, making it a key defensive site.
 
• The construction of Tughlaqabad reflects the ambition of Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq to establish a strong and secure capital for his empire.
 
• The city, however, was abandoned within a few years due to water scarcity and a curse attributed to **Nizamuddin Auliya**, a famous Sufi saint of that era.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq:**

 
 
• He founded the **Tughlaq dynasty** after overthrowing the Khilji dynasty in **1320**.
 
• He ruled from **1320 to 1325** and was known for his administrative reforms and military strategies.
 
• He emphasized on strengthening the empire’s defense by building strong forts and walls.
 
 
 
• **Tughlaqabad Fort:**
 
 
• The fort, a significant part of Tughlaqabad, is spread over **6.5 km** and was built using granite, reflecting Indo-Islamic architecture.
 
• The fort has **13 gates**, citadels, palaces, and underground tunnels, showcasing advanced engineering for that period.
 
• It was built in just **four years**, reflecting the swift construction practices under Ghiyasuddin’s rule.
 
 
 
• **Other Tughlaq Contributions:**
 
 
• Ghiyasuddin also started the construction of the **Qutub Minar’s fourth storey**, which was later completed by his successors.
 
• The Tughlaq dynasty made significant contributions to **urban planning, irrigation systems, and trade regulation**.
 
 
 
• **Other Options Explained:**
 
 
• **Alauddin Khilji:** Known for his military campaigns and economic reforms but did not construct Tughlaqabad.
 
• **Firoz Shah Tughlaq:** Known for building canals, mosques, and cities like Firozabad, but not Tughlaqabad.
 
• **Mohammad Bin Tughlaq:** Famous for his experiments, including shifting the capital from Delhi to Daulatabad, but not for constructing Tughlaqabad.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Architectural Style:** Tughlaqabad is an excellent example of **medieval military architecture**, focusing on defense and strategic positioning.
 
• **Nizamuddin Auliya’s Curse:** A legend states that Nizamuddin Auliya cursed the city, saying, “May it remain uninhabited,” which is often linked to its eventual abandonment.
 
• **Water Scarcity:** The lack of a reliable water source contributed to the city's abandonment despite its strong fortifications.
 
• **Current Status:** Tughlaqabad is now a historical ruin and a popular tourist destination, managed by the **Archaeological Survey of India (ASI)**.

__
 
• **IIT Kanpur** has developed an advanced **solar dehydration technology** to assist farmers by reducing **post-harvest losses** and boosting their income.
 
• This technology uses **solar energy** to dehydrate perishable agricultural products such as fruits, vegetables, and other crops, thereby extending their shelf life.
 
• The initiative is aimed at addressing the challenges of **food wastage** due to lack of proper storage and preservation methods in rural areas.
 
• The solar dehydration technology is cost-efficient, eco-friendly, and specifically designed to be accessible for **small and marginal farmers**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **About IIT Kanpur:**

 
 
• Located in **Kanpur, Uttar Pradesh**, IIT Kanpur is one of India’s premier institutes for engineering and technology.
 
• It was established in **1959** and is renowned for its cutting-edge research and innovation.
 
• Over the years, IIT Kanpur has contributed significantly to advancements in **renewable energy** and agricultural technology.
 
 
 
• **Solar Dehydration Technology:**
 
 
• Solar dehydration is a process of using **solar energy** to remove moisture from agricultural products, preserving them for longer durations.
 
• It is an **eco-friendly and cost-effective** solution compared to conventional drying methods that rely on electricity or fossil fuels.
 
• The technology helps minimize **post-harvest losses**, which are a major issue in India, where approximately 30-40% of produce is wasted annually.
 
 
 
• **Benefits for Farmers:**

questions.question: The Expert Group under the Chairmanship of Dr. C. Rangarajan to Review the Methodology for Measurement of Poverty in the country was constituted by the Planning Commission in___________.

__
 
• The **Expert Group under Dr. C. Rangarajan** was constituted by the **Planning Commission of India in 2012**.
 
• The purpose of this expert group was to review and recommend a new methodology for the **measurement of poverty** in India.
 
• The group was formed in response to widespread criticism of the **Tendulkar Committee methodology**, which was used earlier for poverty estimation.
 
• Dr. C. Rangarajan, a noted economist and former Governor of the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)**, chaired the committee, ensuring credibility and expertise in its recommendations.
 
• In its report, the committee proposed a new methodology for measuring poverty based on **consumption expenditure, nutritional needs, and other socio-economic factors**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• The Planning Commission of India, established in **1950**, was tasked with formulating India's five-year plans for economic development.
 
• It was replaced by the **NITI Aayog** in **2015** to better align with the needs of modern governance and policy implementation.
 
 
 
• **Poverty Measurement in India:**
 
 
• Earlier, the **Alagh Committee (1979)** and **Tendulkar Committee (2009)** provided methodologies for poverty estimation.
 
• The **Tendulkar Committee** methodology faced criticism for setting a very low poverty line, which many argued underestimated India's poverty levels.
 
 
 
• **Rangarajan Committee Recommendations:**
 
 
• The **Rangarajan Committee** proposed a higher poverty line compared to the Tendulkar method, considering a more realistic assessment of minimum consumption needs.

• Dr. Rangarajan is a noted Indian economist and former **Chairman of the Economic Advisory Council to the Prime Minister**.
 
• He also served as the **Governor of the Reserve Bank of India** from **1992 to 1997**.
 
 
 
• **Criticism of Tendulkar Committee:**
 
 
• The poverty line of Rs. 27.2 per capita per day for rural areas (and Rs. 33.3 for urban areas) was considered unrealistically low.
 
• It failed to account for essential non-food expenses like health and education.
 
 
 
• **Post-Rangarajan Developments:**
 
 
• The **NITI Aayog** is now responsible for poverty-related policies and measurements, with a focus on multidimensional poverty.
 
• India adopted the **Global Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI)** to measure poverty more comprehensively.

• The annexation occurred following the **Battle of Miani** on **February 17, 1843**, where Sir Charles Napier defeated the Talpur rulers of Sindh.
 
• The primary reason for annexing Sindh was its **strategic location along the Indus River**, which was vital for trade and military purposes.
 
• After the annexation, Sindh was made a part of the **Bombay Presidency**, and Charles Napier became its first Governor.

• It was fought on **February 17, 1843**, between the British forces led by Sir Charles Napier and the Talpur rulers of Sindh.
 
• The British emerged victorious, which directly led to the annexation of Sindh.
 
• The battle is considered one of the major turning points in the British conquest of India.
 
 
 
• **Sir Charles Napier:**
 
 
• He was a British Army officer and colonial administrator who played a key role in the annexation of Sindh.
 
• Napier is often remembered for his controversial governance and military strategies in the region.

• **Strategic Importance of Sindh:**
 
 
• Sindh's location along the **Indus River** made it a key region for trade and military logistics.
 
• The British sought control over the Indus River to establish a trade route and strengthen their hold in northwest India.
 
• It also served as a buffer zone against potential invasions from the northwest.
 
 
 
• **Impact of the Annexation:**
 
 
• The annexation of Sindh marked the expansion of British rule in northwest India.

• The Talpur dynasty ruled Sindh before its annexation by the British.
 
• They were known for their administrative and military capabilities but were unable to withstand British military advancements.
 
 
 
• **Bombay Presidency:**
 
 
• Sindh was integrated into the Bombay Presidency after annexation, which was one of the major administrative divisions of British India.
 
• This integration facilitated British control over the region and its resources.
 
 
 
• **Economic Exploitation:**
 
 
• The British exploited Sindh's resources, particularly its fertile lands and trade routes.
 
• The annexation also led to significant socio-economic changes in the region.

• Underwriting is a critical function in the primary market, ensuring that companies issuing securities are able to raise the required capital even if the public subscription falls short.
 
• The **SEBI (Underwriters) Regulations, 1993** were introduced to bring in transparency, accountability, and an organized structure to the underwriting process.

• **Underwriters:**

• **Primary Market vs. Secondary Market:**

questions.question:
The Petroleum reserves of India are in which of the following region?

II. Off-shore region in the Arabian sea
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Both I and II**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Petroleum reserves in India** are primarily concentrated in the **sedimentary basins of Assam** and the **off-shore regions in the Arabian Sea**, making these two regions significant contributors to India's crude oil production.
 
• The **sedimentary basins of Assam** have long been known for their petroleum deposits. The **Dibrugarh and Tinsukia districts** host major oilfields such as Digboi, Bongaigaon, and Moran. *Hence, statement I is correct.*
 
• The **offshore region in the Arabian Sea** includes the **Bombay High**, India's largest offshore oilfield. It is managed by the **Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC)** and contributes significantly to India’s crude oil output. *Hence, statement II is correct.*
 
• India has a total of **26 sedimentary basins**, out of which **7 are currently producing oil**. These basins are divided into **onshore and offshore areas**.
 
• The petroleum reserves in these regions play a vital role in fulfilling the energy needs of the nation, reducing dependency on imports.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Petroleum Reserves in Assam:**

 
 
• The **Digboi oilfield**, located in Assam, is the oldest oilfield in Asia and is still operational.
 
• Major oilfields in Assam include **Duliajan, Moran, Lakwa, and Baghjan**. These oilfields are managed by **Oil India Limited (OIL)**.
 
• The crude oil extracted from Assam is refined at the **Numaligarh Refinery**, which is one of the most modern refineries in India.
 
• Assam’s oilfields have been crucial for India’s petroleum industry since the late 19th century.
 
 
 
• **Offshore Reserves in the Arabian Sea:**
 
 
• **Bombay High**, discovered in **1974**, is India’s largest offshore oilfield and is located about **160 km off the Mumbai coast**.
 
• Other important offshore fields include **Neelam, Heera, and Bassein**, which also contribute significantly to India's crude oil production.
 
• The Arabian Sea reserves are managed by **ONGC**, which employs advanced technologies for exploration and production.
 
• Offshore production accounts for more than **40% of India's total crude oil output**.
 
 
 
• **India’s Sedimentary Basins:**
 
 
• India has **26 sedimentary basins**, categorized into **onshore and offshore regions**.
 
• Some of the notable onshore basins include **Assam-Arakan, Cambay, and Rajasthan**, while offshore basins include the **Krishna-Godavari Basin** and **Cauvery Basin**.
 
• Exploration and production activities are carried out by organizations such as **ONGC, Oil India Limited, and private sector companies**.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Petroleum Reserves:**
 
 
• Petroleum reserves are vital for meeting India's **energy demands**, which are increasing due to industrialization and urbanization.
 
• India imports approximately **80% of its crude oil**, and domestic reserves help reduce the import dependency.
 
• The petroleum sector significantly contributes to India's **GDP** and employment, especially in regions like Assam and Gujarat.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Bombay High:**

• It contributes approximately **38% of India’s total crude oil production**.
 
• ONGC uses advanced technologies like **Enhanced Oil Recovery (EOR)** to maximize output.
 
 
 
• **Assam Oilfields:**

• The oil produced is refined at **Guwahati, Bongaigaon, and Numaligarh refineries**.
 
• These oilfields are known for their **high-quality crude oil**.
 
 
 
• **Krishna-Godavari Basin:**
 
 
• Located in Andhra Pradesh, it is one of the richest offshore reserves.
 
• It has significant deposits of **natural gas and crude oil**.
 
• Production from this basin contributes to India’s **energy security**.

• The model developed by **Prasanta Chandra Mahalanobis** focused on the importance of **heavy industries** for long-term growth.

• **Key Industries Developed:**

questions.question:
Which of the following factor affect the distribution of population?

I. Topography

II. Climate
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Both I and II**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Topography:**

 
 
• The physical layout of land, such as mountains, plateaus, and plains, significantly influences the **distribution of population**.
 
• People generally prefer living in plains and river valleys due to their **suitability for agriculture, transportation, and industrial development**. Examples include the Indo-Gangetic Plains in India.
 
• Mountainous regions, such as the Himalayas, usually have **sparse populations** due to harsh climatic conditions, difficult terrain, and lack of economic opportunities.
 
• Hence, topography plays a crucial role in determining where people settle. *Statement I is correct.*
 
 
 
• **Climate:**
 
 
• Climate is a critical factor in population distribution because extreme climates (too hot or too cold) deter settlement.
 
• Regions with **moderate and favorable climates**, such as temperate regions, tend to have higher population densities. For instance, coastal areas in India and Europe are densely populated due to their favorable climate.
 
• In contrast, **extreme climates**, such as deserts (e.g., the Thar Desert) and polar regions, have sparse populations due to the challenges posed by their environmental conditions.
 
• Thus, climate is a significant determinant of population distribution. *Statement II is correct.*
 
 
 
• **Combined Influence:**
 
 
• Topography and climate often interact to shape population patterns. For instance, fertile plains with moderate climates (e.g., the Nile River Valley) are highly populated.
 
• In contrast, mountainous regions with harsh climates (e.g., the Andes or the Himalayas) are sparsely populated.
 
• As both factors collectively influence population distribution, the correct answer is **Both I and II**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Other Factors Affecting Population Distribution:**

 
 
• **Economic Factors:** Regions with industrial hubs, trade centers, and economic opportunities (e.g., Mumbai or New York) attract higher populations.
 
• **Social and Cultural Factors:** Areas with rich cultural heritage or social amenities like education and healthcare services (e.g., Paris or Delhi) are more densely populated.
 
• **Political Stability:** Politically stable regions tend to have higher population densities compared to conflict-prone zones (e.g., Syria or Afghanistan).
 
• **Natural Resources:** Availability of resources like water, minerals, and fertile land supports higher population densities (e.g., the Ruhr region in Germany).
 
 
 
• **Examples of Population Distribution:**
 
 
• High Population Density: The Indo-Gangetic Plain (India) and the Nile River Valley (Egypt).
 
• Low Population Density: The Sahara Desert (Africa) and Siberia (Russia).
 
 
 
• **Key Statistics:**
 
 
• As per the **2023 UN Population Report**, around **56% of the global population lives in urban areas**, primarily due to economic opportunities and better living conditions.
 
• The world’s most populated regions include **South Asia** (e.g., India and Bangladesh) and **East Asia** (e.g., China and Japan).
 
 
 
• **Implications of Population Distribution:**
 
 
• Regions with high population densities often face challenges such as resource depletion, environmental degradation, and urban overcrowding.
 
• Areas with sparse populations might struggle with underdevelopment, lack of infrastructure, and economic stagnation.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **World’s Least Populated Areas:** Antarctica, Arctic regions, and parts of the Sahara Desert.
 
• **World’s Most Populated Cities:** Tokyo (Japan), Delhi (India), Shanghai (China), and São Paulo (Brazil).

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a push factor of migration?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Better job opportunities**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Push factors** refer to conditions that drive people to leave their home regions. These factors are typically negative and forceful, such as **unemployment, poor living conditions, or political turmoil**.
 
• **Unemployment**: Lack of job opportunities in a region can lead individuals to migrate to areas with better employment prospects. This is a **push factor**.
 
• **Poor living conditions**: Issues like lack of access to healthcare, education, or basic amenities can motivate individuals to leave their current location. This is considered a **push factor**.
 
• **Political turmoil**: Instability caused by conflict, oppression, or lack of personal safety can drive people to migrate. This is a **push factor**.
 
• **Better job opportunities**: This is a **pull factor**, as it attracts individuals to migrate to a specific region offering better economic prospects and work conditions. It is NOT a push factor.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Push and Pull Factors:**

 
 
• Push factors are negative conditions in the origin region that compel individuals to migrate, such as **poverty, natural disasters, or persecution**.
 
• Pull factors are positive conditions in the destination region that attract individuals, such as **better economic opportunities, safety, or access to resources**.
 
 
 
• **Examples of Push Factors:**
 
 
• **Natural disasters:** Events like floods, earthquakes, or droughts can force people to leave their homes.
 
• **Conflict:** Political or social unrest can drive individuals to migrate in search of safety.
 
• **Poverty:** Lack of financial resources or economic opportunities is a major reason for migration.
 
 
 
• **Examples of Pull Factors:**
 
 
• **Economic opportunities:** Availability of jobs and better wages can attract migrants.
 
• **Quality of life:** Access to healthcare, education, and infrastructure in developed regions can serve as pull factors.
 
• **Safety:** Political stability and low crime rates in a destination region can attract migrants.
 
 
 
• **Global Migration Trends:**
 
 
• According to the **World Migration Report 2022** by the **International Organization for Migration (IOM)**, around **281 million people** were international migrants in 2020.
 
• The report identifies **economic opportunities** and **climate change** as significant drivers of migration globally.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Economic migration:**

 
 
• This type of migration is often driven by the promise of better job opportunities and higher wages.
 
• Countries with robust economies, like **the United States, Canada, and Australia**, often attract economic migrants.
 
 
 
• **Refugee migration:**
 
 
• Refugees often migrate due to **push factors** like political persecution, war, or natural disasters.
 
• The **United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR)** reported that **89.3 million people** were forcibly displaced worldwide as of 2021.

questions.question: What becomes the major driving force in the movement of water in the xylem during the day?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Transpiration pull**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• **Transpiration pull** is the major driving force for the movement of water through the xylem during the day.
 
• It occurs due to the evaporation of water from the surface of leaves, creating a negative pressure or suction force in the xylem vessels.
 
• This negative pressure helps in pulling water upward from the roots to the leaves, overcoming gravity.
 
• The cohesive and adhesive properties of water molecules play a crucial role in maintaining the continuous column of water in the xylem.
 
• **Transpiration pull** is most effective during the day due to higher rates of transpiration under sunlight and warmer temperatures.

questions.question: What is the primary function of the growth hormone in humans?

options.text: Controls metabolism of carbohydrates and fats
Regulates growth and development of the body

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Regulates growth and development of the body**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Growth hormone (GH), also known as somatotropin**, is a peptide hormone produced by the anterior pituitary gland. Its primary function is to **regulate growth and development in humans**, especially during childhood and adolescence.
 
• GH stimulates the liver to produce **insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1)**, which promotes the growth of bones, muscles, and tissues by enhancing cell division and protein synthesis.
 
• **Bone growth**: Growth hormone plays a critical role in the elongation of long bones during the developmental phase, contributing to increased height. It regulates the activity of growth plates in bones.
 
• **Muscle development**: GH enhances the synthesis of proteins, leading to muscle growth and repair. It also supports the metabolism of fats to provide energy for muscle development.
 
• **Cell regeneration**: Growth hormone facilitates tissue repair and cell regeneration, ensuring the proper functioning of vital organs and systems in the body.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Production and regulation of growth hormone:**

 
 
• GH is secreted by the **anterior pituitary gland**, located at the base of the brain. The hypothalamus regulates its production using two hormones: **growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH)** and **somatostatin**.
 
• Its secretion is **pulsatile**, with peak levels occurring during sleep, particularly in the early hours of the night.
 
• Factors such as exercise, stress, sleep, and nutrition influence GH secretion.
 
 
 
• **Deficiency of growth hormone:**
 
 
• **GH deficiency** in children can lead to **dwarfism**, characterized by short stature and delayed physical growth.
 
• In adults, GH deficiency may result in **reduced muscle mass, increased fat deposition, and low energy levels.**
 
• Treatment involves **GH replacement therapy**, using synthetic growth hormone.
 
 
 
• **Excess of growth hormone:**
 
 
• Excess GH during childhood can cause **gigantism**, leading to abnormally tall stature due to excessive bone growth.
 
• In adults, excess GH results in **acromegaly**, a condition marked by abnormal growth of bones in the face, hands, and feet.
 
• Both conditions require medical intervention, such as surgery or medication, to control GH levels.
 
 
 
• **Other functions of growth hormone:**
 
 
• GH indirectly supports **metabolism** by promoting the breakdown of fats (lipolysis) and regulating carbohydrate metabolism to maintain energy balance.
 
• It helps in maintaining **bone density** and supports the immune system by facilitating cell growth and repair.
 
 
 
• **Applications in medical science:**
 
 
• GH is used in treating **growth hormone deficiency** and certain conditions like Turner syndrome and chronic kidney disease in children.
 
• Recombinant human growth hormone (rhGH) is widely utilized in clinical therapies.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Growth hormone disorders:**

 
 
• **Gigantism** and **acromegaly** result from excessive GH secretion due to pituitary tumors.
 
• **Panhypopituitarism**, a condition of reduced pituitary function, can lead to GH deficiency.
 
 
 
• **Impact of aging:**
 
 
• GH levels naturally decline with age, contributing to reduced muscle mass, increased fat deposition, and diminished physical performance.
 
• Some studies explore the use of GH in managing age-related decline, but its long-term effects remain controversial.
 
 
 
• **Ethical concerns:**
 
 
• Using GH for non-medical purposes, such as enhancing athletic performance, raises ethical and health concerns.
 
• GH misuse can lead to severe health complications, including diabetes and cardiovascular issues.

questions.question: During whose reign was the second Buddhist council was held?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Kalashoka**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Second Buddhist Council** was held during the reign of **Kalashoka** around **383 BCE**, approximately 100 years after the Buddha's Mahaparinirvana.
 
• The council took place at **Vaishali**, a prominent city during ancient times and a key Buddhist center.
 
• The primary purpose of this council was to address disputes among the Buddhist Sangha regarding **Vinaya rules** (disciplinary codes).
 
• The conflicts arose due to certain monks from Vaishali proposing **ten controversial practices**, including accepting gold and silver, which were against the original teachings of the Buddha.
 
• The council ultimately decided in favor of the orthodox views, rejecting the proposed relaxation of monastic rules, and emphasized adherence to the original Vinaya.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Kalashoka:**

 
 
• Kalashoka was a ruler of the **Shishunaga dynasty**, which succeeded the Haryanka dynasty in Magadha.
 
• He was known for his support and patronage of Buddhism and played a significant role in convening the **Second Buddhist Council**.
 
• Kalashoka shifted the Magadhan capital from Rajagriha to **Pataliputra**, which became an important administrative and cultural center.
 
 
 
• **Significance of the Second Buddhist Council:**
 
 
• The council marked the first major schism in Buddhism, leading to the formation of two groups: the **Theravada (Sthaviravada)** and the **Mahasanghikas**.
 
• The **Theravada** group adhered strictly to the original teachings and rules, while the Mahasanghikas advocated for certain changes to accommodate evolving social contexts.
 
• This division laid the foundation for later developments in Buddhist philosophy and practices.
 
 
 
• **First Buddhist Council:**
 
 
• Held at **Rajagriha** (modern Rajgir) under the patronage of King **Ajatashatru**, shortly after the Buddha's death.
 
• The council aimed to compile the Buddha's teachings, resulting in the formation of the **Sutta Pitaka** and **Vinaya Pitaka**.
 
 
 
• **Subsequent Buddhist Councils:**
 
 
• The **Third Buddhist Council** was held under the patronage of Emperor **Ashoka** around 250 BCE at Pataliputra, focusing on resolving doctrinal disputes and spreading Buddhism beyond India.
 
• The **Fourth Buddhist Council** was convened in Kashmir during the reign of **Kanishka** (1st century CE) and was instrumental in shaping the Mahayana tradition.
 
 
 
• **Vinaya Pitaka:**
 
 
• The Vinaya Pitaka contains rules and regulations for monastic life and is a key component of the Buddhist canon.
 
• Disputes over interpretations of these rules were the primary reason for convening the Second Buddhist Council.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Ajatashatru:**

 
 
• King of Magadha during the time of the **First Buddhist Council**.
 
• Played a crucial role in the early consolidation of Buddhism by supporting the compilation of the Buddha's teachings.
 
 
 
• **Bimbisara:**
 
 
• Predecessor of Ajatashatru and one of the earliest patrons of the Buddha.
 
• His reign marked the beginning of significant royal support for Buddhism.
 
 
 
• **Mahapadma Nanda:**
 
 
• Founder of the **Nanda dynasty**, which succeeded the Shishunaga dynasty.
 
• Did not have any direct association with the Buddhist councils.
